ground_truth: Cyst formation in a persistent thyroglossal duct

differential: Thyroglossal Duct Cyst
This is the most common congenital midline neck mass, typically presenting in childhood or adolescence.
Cervical Lymphadenopathy
Enlarged lymph nodes are a very common response to infection or inflammation in this age group.
Thyroid Nodule
A mass in the anterior neck of an adolescent female could represent a growth within the thyroid gland.
Dermoid Cyst
This is a common congenital midline mass resulting from entrapped ectodermal tissue during development.
Lymphoma
This malignancy is a critical consideration for any persistent neck mass in an adolescent.
eliminated: Zenker's diverticulum
This is a condition of older adults and is not seen in a 13-year-old.
Metastatic Squamous Cell Carcinoma
This malignancy is associated with risk factors and an age group not consistent with this patient.

differential: Thyroglossal duct cyst
This is the most common congenital midline neck mass in children, and it classically moves with swallowing.
Dermoid cyst
This congenital cyst is a common cause of a non-tender, fluctuant midline neck mass in the submental region.
Plunging ranula
A mucocele from the sublingual gland can dissect inferiorly through the mylohyoid muscle to present as a cystic midline neck mass.
Lymphatic malformation
This congenital anomaly of the lymphatic system can present as a soft, fluctuant, non-tender mass in the neck.
Submental lymphadenopathy
An enlarged lymph node could present as a midline mass, though fluctuance without signs of infection is less common.
eliminated: Branchial cleft cyst
The midline location of the mass is inconsistent with a branchial cleft cyst, which is typically found laterally on the neck.
Thyroid goiter
The mass is located superior to the hyoid bone, which is above the typical location of the thyroid gland.
Cervical abscess
The absence of pain, erythema, and fever makes an acute infectious abscess highly unlikely.

This developmental anomaly can present as a midline mass that moves with swallowing, although normal thyroid function tests make it less probable.

differential: Thyroglossal duct cyst
This is the confirmed diagnosis, fitting the classic presentation of a painless, midline neck mass that moves with swallowing and has a characteristic tract to the tongue base on ultrasound.
Dermoid cyst
This is a common congenital midline neck mass in children, which can present as a painless, fluctuant swelling in the submental region.
Ectopic thyroid tissue
This diagnosis is considered for any midline neck mass, as it represents thyroid tissue located along the path of embryonic descent.
Lymphadenopathy
Swollen lymph nodes are a very common cause of neck masses, although the midline location and cystic feel are less typical.
Branchial cleft cyst
Although usually located laterally, these congenital cysts can occasionally present near the midline and must be considered in the differential for a pediatric neck mass.
eliminated: Neck abscess
The absence of fever, pain, erythema, and the normal white blood cell count make an acute infectious process unlikely.
Thyroid goiter
The location of the mass superior to the hyoid bone is not consistent with the typical location of the thyroid gland.

differential: Thyroglossal Duct Cyst
This is a very common congenital midline neck mass in children and adolescents.
Thyroid Nodule
The location is consistent with a nodule arising from the thyroid gland, a key structure in the anterior neck.
Cervical Lymphadenopathy
Enlarged lymph nodes are a frequent cause of neck masses in this age group, often due to reactive or infectious causes.
Goiter
The "lump" could represent a diffusely enlarged thyroid gland, which can occur in adolescent females due to various thyroid disorders.
Dermoid Cyst
This is a congenital cyst that can present as a midline neck mass in a young person.
eliminated: Branchial Cleft Cyst
These typically present as a lateral neck mass, not on the front of the neck.

differential: Infected thyroglossal duct cyst
This is the most common congenital midline neck mass in children, and its movement with swallowing and signs of infection are classic.
Infected dermoid cyst
This is another common congenital midline neck mass that can present with tenderness, fluctuance, and erythema when secondarily infected.
Suppurative lymphadenitis
Infection of submental lymph nodes can lead to a tender, fluctuant, and erythematous mass in the midline suprahyoid region.
Dental abscess
An abscess from a mandibular tooth can track inferiorly to present as a tender, fluctuant submental mass with overlying erythema.
Infected epidermal inclusion cyst
This common cutaneous cyst can become inflamed and infected, presenting as a tender, fluctuant, erythematous nodule on the neck.
eliminated: Lipoma
The findings of fluctuance, tenderness, and erythema are inconsistent with a lipoma, which is typically soft, non-tender, and without overlying skin changes.
Thyroid goiter
The mass is located superior to the hyoid bone, which is outside the typical location of the thyroid gland.

differential: Infected thyroglossal duct cyst
The classic midline location, movement with swallowing, and superimposed signs of infection (tenderness, fluctuance, erythema) make this the most likely diagnosis.
Dermoid cyst
This is a common congenital midline neck mass that can present similarly, especially if it becomes secondarily infected.
Submental abscess
A primary abscess in this location would explain the tender, fluctuant, erythematous mass, although movement with swallowing is less specific.
Suppurative lymphadenitis
Infected submental lymph nodes could coalesce into a fluctuant mass, presenting with localized signs of infection.
Ectopic thyroid gland
While less common, an ectopic thyroid can present as a midline neck mass and can become inflamed or cystic, though the normal TSH makes this less probable.
eliminated: Goiter
The mass is superior to the hyoid bone, which is not the location of the thyroid gland, and thyroid function tests are normal.
Branchial cleft cyst
These are typically located on the lateral aspect of the neck, not in the midline.

differential: Thyroglossal Duct Cyst
This is the confirmed diagnosis based on the classic midline location, movement with swallowing, and ultrasound findings of a cystic structure with a tract to the tongue base.
Dermoid Cyst
A common congenital midline neck mass that can become inflamed, although it typically does not move with swallowing.
Infected Lymphadenopathy
A tender, erythematous, fluctuant mass could represent a suppurative lymph node, though the perfectly midline location is less common.
Ectopic Thyroid Gland
This can present as a midline neck mass, but is less likely given the cystic nature on ultrasound and normal thyroid function tests.
Branchial Cleft Cyst
This is a congenital neck cyst that can become infected, but it typically presents more laterally in the neck.
eliminated: Thyroid Goiter
The mass is located superior to the typical position of the thyroid gland and thyroid function tests were normal.
Cystic Hygroma
The location is atypical for a lymphangioma, which usually presents in the posterior triangle and is more common in infancy.
